items.label: f04-milestone-zero
items.front: Capstone milestone 0: which decisions must the design doc settle before any code?
items.back: 1. Outbox schema (workspace schema or shared core table; the mutation's transaction is on the workspace datasource). 2. Relay design (poller, LISTEN/NOTIFY or hybrid; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). 3. Idempotency key, e.g. (eventId, webhookId). 4. Retry policy and dead letter. 5. Chunking. 6. Back-compat for existing consumers. 7. A per-workspace kill switch.

items.label: f03-flat-entity-pipeline
items.front: Describe ADR-004's flat-entity pipeline and its main cost.
items.back: Every metadata entity has a flat canonical projection (flat-object-metadata, flat-field-metadata, flat-view, ...). A mutation produces the desired flat state; workspace-migration-builder diffs it against actual state and emits typed actions; workspace-migration-runner action handlers execute them. Cost: one new property touches the entity, its flat type, comparator, builder and action handler.

items.label: f01-triple-mortgage
items.front: ADR-002 calls its consequence a 'triple mortgage of bespoke infrastructure'. Name the three pieces.
items.back: Because nothing about the data layer is knowable at compile time: a custom ORM (ADR-005, twenty-orm), a GraphQL schema generator (ADR-006, workspace-schema.factory.ts) and a metadata migration engine (ADR-004, the flat-entity diff/apply). Debugging means joining what the metadata says with what Postgres actually has.

items.label: f02-tenancy-costs
items.front: What does ADR-003 list as the costs of schema-per-workspace tenancy?
items.back: Table count grows as workspaces times objects, and Postgres catalogs, autovacuum and pg_dump degrade with huge table counts; platform upgrades must iterate every workspace with @RegisteredWorkspaceCommand (O(tenants) DDL); one shared database means noisy neighbours share buffer cache and I/O until sharding exists.

items.prompt: What delivery semantics does the reliable-webhooks capstone set as its target?

choices.text: Best-effort delivery, with a daily replay of failed events
Exactly-once delivery, via a transaction around the POST
At-most-once delivery, but with every failure logged
At-least-once delivery that consumers can deduplicate

choices: Best-effort delivery, with a daily replay of failed events
Exactly-once delivery, via a transaction around the POST
At-most-once delivery, but with every failure logged
At-least-once delivery that consumers can deduplicate

items.explanation: The capstone states the target as at-least-once delivery with consumer-side dedupability, and adds that exactly-once is not on the menu (a database transaction cannot include a remote HTTP call). At-most-once is the current behaviour it sets out to fix.

items.prompt: Milestone 1 writes outbox rows in the same transaction as the record mutation. What must its integration test show for a mutation that rolls back?

choices.text: That the relay still dispatches the event, but marked as a draft
That an outbox row remains, flagged as cancelled for the relay
That the outbox row is deleted later by a cleanup cron job
That no outbox row is left behind for the rolled-back mutation

choices: That the relay still dispatches the event, but marked as a draft
That an outbox row remains, flagged as cancelled for the relay
That the outbox row is deleted later by a cleanup cron job
That no outbox row is left behind for the rolled-back mutation

items.explanation: Acceptance (a): a mutation whose transaction rolls back leaves no outbox row; that is the point of writing it in the same transaction. Acceptance (b) is the other half: killing the worker between commit and relay dispatch loses nothing, because the row is picked up on the next relay tick.

items.prompt: ADR-004 rejected event-sourced metadata (state by replaying a change log). What is its argument for diffing against actual state instead?

choices.text: Event sourcing would need a second database just to store the log
Live DDL drifts, so replay goes confidently wrong; a diff self-heals
Replaying the change log was too slow for workspaces with many objects
Postgres cannot replay DDL statements inside one transaction block

choices: Event sourcing would need a second database just to store the log
Live DDL drifts, so replay goes confidently wrong; a diff self-heals
Replaying the change log was too slow for workspaces with many objects
Postgres cannot replay DDL statements inside one transaction block

items.explanation: The ADR says replay assumes the target's real state matches the log, but runtime DDL against a live database drifts (failed steps, manual fixes), so replay produces confident wrongness, whereas diffing against actual state self-heals. Speed, storage and transactional DDL are not the reasons given.

items.prompt: Per ADR-002, how are Twenty's standard objects such as company, person and opportunity defined?

choices.text: As workspace entities seeded into metadata like any custom object
As code-generated classes that are compiled per tenant at signup
As fixed TypeORM tables in core, outside the metadata system
As JSONB documents in one shared records table per workspace

choices: As workspace entities seeded into metadata like any custom object
As code-generated classes that are compiled per tenant at signup
As fixed TypeORM tables in core, outside the metadata system
As JSONB documents in one shared records table per workspace

items.explanation: ADR-002: the standard objects in src/modules/ are workspace entities extending base.workspace-entity.ts and seeded into metadata like any custom object, so standard and custom ride identical rails. Fixed TypeORM entities are only for platform data (users, workspaces, billing); JSONB and per-tenant codegen are rejected alternatives.

items.prompt: ADR-003 rejects shared tables with a workspaceId discriminator column. Why is that option incompatible with ADR-002?

choices.text: A discriminator column cannot be indexed in Postgres partitioned tables
Tenants have different columns, so one shared company table can't exist
Shared tables would need row-level security, which Twenty cannot run
The discriminator would leak workspace ids through the GraphQL schema

choices: A discriminator column cannot be indexed in Postgres partitioned tables
Tenants have different columns, so one shared company table can't exist
Shared tables would need row-level security, which Twenty cannot run
The discriminator would leak workspace ids through the GraphQL schema

items.explanation: Because each workspace defines its own objects and fields (ADR-002), the tables differ per tenant; a shared company table would only work by falling back to JSONB or EAV. RLS is rejected separately for the same reason plus policy-management cost, not because it cannot run.

items.prompt: Lab question 5 lists bookkeeping columns 'id, timestamps, deletedAt, position...'. Which fields does BaseWorkspaceEntity itself declare?

choices.text: id, createdAt, updatedAt and deletedAt, with position not among them
id, createdAt, updatedAt, deletedAt and position, in that order
id and position only, while the timestamps come from the metadata module
id, createdAt and updatedAt; deletedAt is added per object type

choices: id, createdAt, updatedAt and deletedAt, with position not among them
id, createdAt, updatedAt, deletedAt and position, in that order
id and position only, while the timestamps come from the metadata module
id, createdAt and updatedAt; deletedAt is added per object type

items.explanation: base.workspace-entity.ts declares exactly four fields: id, createdAt, updatedAt and deletedAt (string | null). position is not in the base class, so if your new table has it, it came from elsewhere. The lab says to confirm rather than assume; the code is keyed here, not the lab's parenthesis.

items.prompt: ADR-002 serves every request from a cached per-workspace projection of the metadata. What does it say a stale cache becomes?

choices.text: An API-correctness bug, not merely a performance problem
Nothing visible, as each request re-reads the metadata tables
A cosmetic issue, since only the Settings UI reads from that cache
A performance issue only, since Postgres stays the source of truth

choices: An API-correctness bug, not merely a performance problem
Nothing visible, as each request re-reads the metadata tables
A cosmetic issue, since only the Settings UI reads from that cache
A performance issue only, since Postgres stays the source of truth

items.explanation: The negative consequences say the serving path depends on a cached projection, so cache staleness becomes an API-correctness bug, not a performance bug: the GraphQL schema, ORM and permissions are resolved from it. The cache is versioned per workspace; nothing says requests bypass it or names a one-day TTL.

items.prompt: The capstone's review gate asks: the relay crashes after the POST but before marking the row dispatched. What should the consumer see?

choices.text: An error response, as the consumer rejects any unmarked events
A single delivery, since the row was already sent once
A duplicate delivery, which is why the idempotency key exists
Nothing new, since the relay's lock rolls the POST back

choices: An error response, as the consumer rejects any unmarked events
A single delivery, since the row was already sent once
A duplicate delivery, which is why the idempotency key exists
Nothing new, since the relay's lock rolls the POST back

items.explanation: On the next tick the row is still unmarked, so the relay sends it again: a duplicate. The gate says that if your answer isn't 'a duplicate, which is why the idempotency key exists', go back to the idempotency step. A database lock cannot undo an HTTP request already sent.

items.prompt: ADR-002 lists entity-attribute-value (EAV) tables as a rejected alternative. What reason does it give?

choices.text: It needs a redeploy for every new field a customer adds
EAV cannot store relations between two custom objects at all
Postgres caps how many rows one EAV attribute table is allowed to hold
Query complexity explodes with self-joins, and indexes become useless

choices: It needs a redeploy for every new field a customer adds
EAV cannot store relations between two custom objects at all
Postgres caps how many rows one EAV attribute table is allowed to hold
Query complexity explodes with self-joins, and indexes become useless

items.explanation: The ADR says EAV makes query complexity explode (multi-way self-joins), makes indexes useless, and ends with reimplementing a planner in app code. The redeploy objection belongs to the code-generation alternative, and the ADR claims no row cap or relation limit.

items.prompt: A metadata change fails halfway: some DDL ran, some did not. What does ADR-004 say happens when the operation is simply run again?

choices.text: It reapplies every action, relying on IF NOT EXISTS guards
It refuses until an operator marks the metadata as repaired
It computes and applies only the delta that is still missing
It rolls back the applied DDL first, then replays all of it

choices: It reapplies every action, relying on IF NOT EXISTS guards
It refuses until an operator marks the metadata as repaired
It computes and applies only the delta that is still missing
It rolls back the applied DDL first, then replays all of it

items.explanation: The positive consequence is retry-is-repair: after partial failure, re-running diffs desired against actual state and computes only the remaining delta, so convergence is a design property. The ADR explains that two-phase commit across metadata and DDL is not available, so there is no rollback-and-replay step.

items.prompt: Under schema-per-workspace tenancy, what would a bug have to do to read another workspace's records?

choices.text: Build a query that names the other workspace's schema explicitly
Reuse a pooled connection whose search_path still points elsewhere
Leave out the WHERE workspaceId = ? predicate in a shared query
Pass a record id from the other workspace into the GraphQL resolver

choices: Build a query that names the other workspace's schema explicitly
Reuse a pooled connection whose search_path still points elsewhere
Leave out the WHERE workspaceId = ? predicate in a shared query
Pass a record id from the other workspace into the GraphQL resolver

items.explanation: ADR-003 says isolation is structural: a query physically targets one schema, so leakage requires constructing a wrong schema name, not forgetting a WHERE clause. The SQL lab's Part 4 asks you to verify that no shared table exists where a missing predicate leaks rows. A foreign record id simply is not in your schema's tables.

items.prompt: Lab Part 1 asks what naming convention marks a workspace schema. What does getWorkspaceSchemaName return for a workspace id?

choices.text: The workspace's subdomain, lowercased and stripped of any dots
workspace_ followed by the workspace UUID re-encoded in base 36
workspace_ followed by the raw UUID with its hyphens removed
ws_ followed by the first eight hex digits of the workspace UUID

choices: The workspace's subdomain, lowercased and stripped of any dots
workspace_ followed by the workspace UUID re-encoded in base 36
workspace_ followed by the raw UUID with its hyphens removed
ws_ followed by the first eight hex digits of the workspace UUID

items.explanation: The util is a one-liner: return `workspace_${uuidToBase36(workspaceId)}`. So the suffix encodes the workspace UUID in base 36, which keeps the name short and valid as a Postgres identifier. Neither the subdomain nor a truncated hex prefix is used.
